title: 出門走走

grammar.title: 搭／坐／騎 + 車 + 去／來 + 地方
grammar.pattern: 主語 + 搭／坐／騎 + 交通工具 + 去／來 + 地方
grammar.explanation: In Mandarin the means of transport is said BEFORE the motion verb. First say how you travel (搭捷運、坐飛機、騎腳踏車), then say 去 or 來 plus the place. 去 means moving away from where the speaker is; 來 means moving toward the speaker.
grammar.contrast: 去 vs 來: both follow the transport phrase, but the choice depends on where the speaker is standing. If you are at the café and your friend is coming to you, say 搭捷運來咖啡廳; if you are at home talking about going there, say 搭捷運去咖啡廳.
grammar.common_error: Learners copy English word order ('go to the station by taxi') and say 我去火車站搭計程車, which actually means 'I go to the station to catch a taxi'. Put the transport first: 我搭計程車去火車站.

examples.gloss: I take the MRT to the train station.

examples.pinyin: Tā qí jiǎotàchē lái wǒ jiā.
examples.gloss: She comes to my place by bike.

examples.hanzi: 爸爸坐飛機去日本工作。
examples.pinyin: Bàba zuò fēijī qù Rìběn gōngzuò.
examples.gloss: Dad flies to Japan for work.

grammar.title: 在 + 地方（人在哪裡）
grammar.explanation: 在 before a place name says where someone or something is right now. No other verb is needed: 我在火車站 already means 'I am at the train station'.
grammar.contrast: 在 marks a static location; 去／來 mark movement. 我在火車站 = I'm there already; 我去火車站 = I'm heading there.
grammar.common_error: Learners add an extra 'be' verb and say 我是在火車站. Drop 是 — 在 is the verb.

examples.gloss: I'm near the train station right now.
The boss isn't in the shop.

grammar.title: Saying where something is: A 在 B 前面/後面
grammar.pattern: A + 在 + B + 前面/後面 (also: A + 在 + 這裡/那裡/哪裡)
grammar.explanation: To say where something is, put the thing first, then 在, then the reference place, and put the location word 前面 or 後面 AFTER that place. So 「書店」+「前面」= 在書店前面 (in front of the bookstore). 這裡 / 那裡 / 哪裡 are place words on their own, so they go straight after 在: 我在這裡、他在那裡、你在哪裡?
grammar.contrast: 這/那/哪 vs 這裡/那裡/哪裡: bare 這、那、哪 point at a thing and come before a noun or classifier (這本書、那家店、哪一個), while 這裡、那裡、哪裡 are places and come after 在 or 去. Ask yourself: am I naming a thing, or a spot?
grammar.common_error: Learners copy English word order and say 在前面書店 ("in front of the bookstore"). In Chinese the place comes first and 前面/後面 comes last: 在書店前面. The other frequent slip is 你在哪? for a location — use 你在哪裡?, because 哪 alone cannot follow 在.

passage.title: 我家附近
passage.hanzi: 我家附近有好多店。前面有一家便利商店,後面有一個郵局和一家書店。我喜歡那裡的咖啡廳,晚上會在那裡看書、寫日記。朋友說這裡的捷運站太遠,我說不遠喔,在學校前面,走路十分鐘。
passage.gloss: There are lots of shops near my home. In front there's a convenience store, and behind there's a post office and a bookstore. I like the café over there; in the evening I read and write in my diary there. A friend says the MRT station here is too far, but I say it isn't far at all — it's in front of the school, a ten-minute walk.

grammar.title: 上／下 for the previous and next time period
grammar.pattern: 上／下 + 星期／個月／年 ；上／下 + 車／班
grammar.explanation: 上 means 'the one before' and 下 means 'the one after'. Put them in front of a week, month or year word: 上星期 = last week, 下星期 = next week, 上個月 = last month, 下個月 = next month. The same 上／下 pair also works with vehicles and work: 上車 (get on), 下車 (get off), 上班 (go to work), 下班 (get off work). Note 上午 and 下午 (morning / afternoon) follow the same up-down feeling.
grammar.contrast: With days, Mandarin does NOT use 上／下 — it uses 前／後: 前天 (the day before yesterday), 昨天, 明天, 後天 (the day after tomorrow). The unit decides: 天 takes 前／後, but 星期／個月／年 take 上／下.
grammar.common_error: Learners say 上天 or 下天 for 'yesterday / tomorrow', and sometimes put the word after the noun (星期下). Keep 上／下 in front: 上星期, 下個月, and use 昨天／明天 for days.

passage.title: 我家附近
passage.hanzi: 我住在台中，我家附近有一間小飯館。那間飯館的麵太好吃了，我下班後都去吃。飯館後面是郵局，郵局前面有一間醫院。上星期我頭痛，去醫院看了醫生。回家的路上，我在捷運站看見飯館的老闆，他請我吃麵。
passage.gloss: I live in Taichung, and there is a small restaurant near my home. The noodles at that restaurant are so good that I go there after work every day. Behind the restaurant is the post office, and in front of the post office there is a hospital. Last week I had a headache, so I went to the hospital to see a doctor. On the way home I saw the restaurant's boss at the MRT station, and he treated me to noodles.
